guide.title: The Castro, San Francisco: the Castro Theatre, the Rainbow Honor Walk and Corona Heights
guide.intro: The Castro is a small district in central San Francisco whose core is Castro Street between Market and 19th Streets. The Castro Theatre stands at 429 Castro Street: San Francisco Landmark No. 100, designated in 1977 under Article 10 of the Planning Code. Harvey Milk ran a camera shop and a political campaign from 573-575 Castro Street, and bronze plaques set into the sidewalks of those blocks carry the Rainbow Honor Walk and the Castro Street History Walk. The district also holds two museums, one of them standing inside a 13.25-acre park whose summit is exposed red chert; a public library; a Catholic parish with published Mass times; a hardware store that moved into the remodelled 1910 Castro Theatre building in 1971; and a Wednesday farmers' market on Noe Street.

sections.heading: Castro Street between Market and 19th
sections.body:
Twin Peaks Tavern is at 401 Castro Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 264, designated in 2012. The Bank of Italy Branch Building at 400-410 Castro Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 325, designated in 2026. Above the entrance to Castro station, the rainbow flag and its flagpole at Harvey Milk Plaza are San Francisco Landmark No. 319, designated in 2024; the plaza was dedicated to Milk in 1985 and the flagpole was added in 1997, for the twentieth anniversary of his election. Pink Triangle Park and Memorial stands at Castro, Market and 17th Streets.

Walking south from Market, the addresses come quickly. The Castro Theatre is at 429 Castro Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 100, designated in 1977; the ordinance that amended the designation in 2023 names the property 429-431 Castro Street. Cliff's Variety is at 471-479 Castro Street. The San Francisco AIDS Foundation building at 514-520 Castro Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 333, designated in 2026. Castro Camera, where Harvey Milk kept his shop and his flat, is at 573-575 Castro Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 227, designated in 2000, and the Castro Rock Steam Baths at 578-582 Castro Street are San Francisco Landmark No. 326, designated in 2026.

The sidewalks themselves are the other thing to look at. The Rainbow Honor Walk sets bronze plaques into the pavement, and the Castro Street History Walk adds twenty historical fact plaques contained within the 400 and 500 blocks of Castro Street, between 19th and Market. Both sit in paving laid by the Castro Street Streetscape Improvement Project, which San Francisco Public Works records as completed, on Castro Street between Market and 19th Streets, with a budget of ten million dollars in District 8, funded by the 2011 Road Repaving and Street Safety Bond and the Federal Transportation Administration. The same project page names special paving and barrier improvements at Jane Warner Plaza, the pedestrian plaza at the streetcar turnaround.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Castro station opened in 1980 and is served by the Muni Metro K, L, M and S lines. Its main entrance is below Harvey Milk Plaza, where Market, Castro and 17th Streets meet. The F Market heritage streetcar line turns around at Market and 17th Streets. No source states a journey time or a distance between any two addresses in the district, so steer by the addresses themselves.

The ones worth writing down: the Castro Theatre at 429 Castro Street; the GLBT Historical Society Museum at 4127 18th Street; Cliff's Variety at 471-479 Castro Street; the Castro Country Club at 4058 18th Street; the Eureka Valley / Harvey Milk Memorial Branch Library at 1 Jose Sarria Court; Most Holy Redeemer at 100 Diamond Street; and the Castro Farmers' Market at 270 Noe Street.

Corona Heights Park and the Randall Museum share an entrance address at 199 Museum Way, and the Recreation and Parks Department gives the park entrance as Roosevelt and Museum Way. The museum stands inside the park, and the park adjoins Buena Vista Park. Note that the steps leading up to the peak of Corona Heights are not supported by handrails.

sections.heading: Hours, admission and Mass times
sections.body:
The Randall Museum opens Tuesday through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed Sunday and Monday, and admission is free; Cafe Josephine inside it opens Tuesday to Friday 9:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. and Saturday 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. The GLBT Historical Society Museum opens Tuesday to Sunday, 11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. and 1:30 p.m. to 5:00 p.m., closed Monday, and is free to all visitors on the first Wednesday of every month, sponsored by the Bob Ross Foundation. The Eureka Valley / Harvey Milk Memorial Branch Library opens Sunday 1 to 5, Monday 10 to 6, Tuesday to Thursday 10 to 8, Friday 1 to 6 and Saturday 10 to 6.

Corona Heights Park gives its hours as 5 a.m. to midnight. The Castro Farmers' Market at 270 Noe Street runs Wednesdays 3:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m., from 1 April 2026 to 18 November 2026. Cliff's Variety opens Monday to Saturday 10:00 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. and Sunday 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. The Castro Country Club opens Sunday to Thursday 7:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., and Friday and Saturday 7:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. The Cafe at 2369 Market Street opens Thursday to Saturday, 9 p.m. to 2 a.m.

Most Holy Redeemer at 100 Diamond Street gives Mass Monday to Friday at 8:00 a.m., a Saturday vigil at 5:00 p.m., Sunday at 8:00 a.m., 10:00 a.m. and 6:30 p.m., holy days at 8:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m., Thanksgiving Day at 10:00 a.m., and reconciliation on Saturdays from 3:45 to 4:30 p.m. The Castro Theatre and the Swedish American Hall both publish live event calendars rather than fixed opening hours. For Twin Peaks Tavern, no source states opening hours, so none are given here.

faq.question: What can a visitor actually go inside?
faq.answer: Two museums, a library, a park, a church and a coffeehouse, all with published hours. The GLBT Historical Society Museum at 4127 18th Street opens Tuesday to Sunday, 11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. and 1:30 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. The Randall Museum at 199 Museum Way opens Tuesday through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., free. The Eureka Valley / Harvey Milk Memorial Branch Library is at 1 Jose Sarria Court. Corona Heights Park gives park hours of 5 a.m. to midnight. Most Holy Redeemer at 100 Diamond Street publishes Mass times. The Castro Country Club at 4058 18th Street, a sober community coffeehouse, opens from 7:00 a.m. daily. The Castro Theatre trades on a live event calendar.

faq.question: What is the Castro Theatre?
faq.answer: A cinema and concert hall at 429 Castro Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 100, designated in 1977 under Article 10 of the Planning Code, and the designation was amended by Ordinance No. 109-23 in 2023, which names the property 429-431 Castro Street. The theatre opened on 22 June 1922 to a design by Timothy L. Pflueger. Its Art Deco marquee was added in 1937. The auditorium seats 1,400 for concerts and 1,150 for films, and the venue publishes a live event calendar.

faq.question: What are the bronze plaques in the sidewalk?
faq.answer: Two separate sets, sharing the same blocks. The Rainbow Honor Walk, founded by David Perry, installed a first round of twenty plaques in 2014 and completed a second round of twenty-four in 2019; twenty-four further honorees were named in 2022. Its own counters give 46 plaques installed and 28 planned, with fundraising continuing. The route runs from the Harvey Milk Civil Rights Academy at 19th and Collingwood along Castro Street to Market, and it branches in both directions at 18th and Castro. The Castro Street History Walk is a separate set of twenty historical fact plaques, ten of them covering the period from before 1776 to the 1960s, contained within the 400 and 500 blocks of Castro Street.

faq.question: Which buildings here carry Article 10 landmark designations?
faq.answer: They are spread across Castro Street, Upper Market and the surrounding blocks. On or near Castro Street: San Francisco Landmark No. 100 (the Castro Theatre), No. 227 (Castro Camera), No. 264 (Twin Peaks Tavern), No. 319 (the rainbow flag at Harvey Milk Plaza), No. 325 (the Bank of Italy branch), No. 326 (the Castro Rock Steam Baths), No. 329 (Full Moon Coffeehouse) and No. 333 (the San Francisco AIDS Foundation building). On Market Street: No. 79 (the Miller-Joost House), No. 241 (the Jose Theater), No. 267 (the Swedish American Hall) and No. 277 (New Era Hall). Elsewhere: No. 39 (Saint Francis Lutheran Church), No. 67 and No. 68 (the Tanforan Cottages), No. 80 (the Clarke Mansion), No. 208 (the McCormick House), No. 255 (Mission High School), No. 284 (the Benedict-Gieling House), No. 322 (the Bob Ross House), No. 323 (Sha'ar Zahav) and No. 335 (St. Nicholas Cathedral).

faq.question: Is anything free?
faq.answer: Admission to the Randall Museum is free. The GLBT Historical Society Museum is free to all visitors on the first Wednesday of every month, sponsored by the Bob Ross Foundation. The Eureka Valley / Harvey Milk Memorial Branch Library and every park cost nothing: Corona Heights at 199 Museum Way, Kite Hill at 10 Stanton Street, Seward Mini Park at 70 Corwin Street, Peixotto Playground at 2475 15th Street, States Street Playground at 122 States Street, and the three mini parks at 299 Henry Street, 70 Ord Street and 1 Beaver Street. Pink Triangle Park and Memorial is open ground at Castro, Market and 17th Streets, and the Rainbow Honor Walk is in the pavement.

places.name: Castro Theatre
places.summary: The cinema and concert hall on the west side of Castro Street, and the building the district is usually pictured by. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 100, designated in 1977 under Article 10 of the Planning Code. The designation was amended by Ordinance No. 109-23 in 2023, which names the property 429-431 Castro Street. Its own site carries a live event calendar rather than fixed opening hours.
places.history: The Castro Theatre opened on 22 June 1922 to a design by Timothy L. Pflueger. Its Art Deco marquee was added in 1937. The auditorium seats 1,400 for concerts and 1,150 for films.

places.name: Castro Camera and the Harvey Milk Residence
places.summary: The storefront where Harvey Milk ran his camera shop and his campaign headquarters, with his flat above it. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 227, designated in 2000.
places.history: A memorial plaque and an interior mural mark the site, and a smaller mural of Milk sits above the sidewalk on the building.

places.name: Twin Peaks Tavern
places.summary: San Francisco Landmark No. 264, designated in 2012. The building stands at the corner of Castro and Market Streets. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The designation covers the plate-glass-windowed corner building itself.

places.name: Harvey Milk Plaza and the Rainbow Flag
places.summary: The open plaza where Market, Castro and 17th Streets meet, above the main entrance to Castro station. The rainbow flag flying over it, together with its flagpole, is San Francisco Landmark No. 319, designated in 2024; the register carries no parcel address for it, because the designation is the flag and the pole rather than a building.
places.history: The plaza was dedicated to Harvey Milk in 1985. The flagpole was added in 1997, for the twentieth anniversary of his election. Castro station beneath it opened in 1980.

places.name: Bank of Italy Branch Building
places.summary: San Francisco Landmark No. 325, designated in 2026, at 400-410 Castro Street, on the corner block where Castro Street meets Market.
places.history: The enacting ordinance is No. 63-26.

places.name: Castro Rock Steam Baths
places.summary: San Francisco Landmark No. 326, designated in 2026, at 578-582 Castro Street.
places.history: The enacting ordinance is No. 64-26.

places.name: San Francisco AIDS Foundation Building
places.summary: San Francisco Landmark No. 333, designated in 2026, at 514-520 Castro Street.
places.history: The enacting ordinance is No. 71-26, carrying a Board of Supervisors memorandum dated 15 May 2026.

places.name: Full Moon Coffeehouse
places.summary: San Francisco Landmark No. 329, designated in 2026, at 4416 18th Street.
places.history: The enacting ordinance is No. 67-26. No source states what occupies the building now, so nothing is said about it.

places.name: Bob Ross House
places.summary: San Francisco Landmark No. 322, designated in 2026, at 4200 20th Street. It is a private house.
places.history: The enacting ordinance is No. 60-26. The Bob Ross Foundation sponsors the free first Wednesday of every month at the GLBT Historical Society Museum.

places.name: Sha'ar Zahav (Historic Location)
places.summary: The building at 220 Danvers Street that Congregation Sha'ar Zahav formerly occupied. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 323, designated in 2026, and the register's name for it carries the words Historic Location. No source states what stands in it today.
places.history: The enacting ordinance is No. 61-26.

places.name: The Jose Theater / NAMES Project Building
places.summary: A Market Street building carrying two names from two chapters of its use. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 241, designated in 2004.
places.history: The theatre was named for Jose Sarria. The building later held the NAMES Project storefront, the organisation behind the AIDS Memorial Quilt.

places.name: Swedish American Hall and Cafe du Nord
places.summary: One building with two room names and one address. San Francisco Landmark No. 267, designated in 2015. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 30 September 2019, reference number 100004413. The venue's own site publishes a live calendar under both the Cafe du Nord and the Swedish American Hall names and gives the address as 2174 Market Street.
places.history: Cafe du Nord occupies the lower level of the building and the hall the upper.

places.name: New Era Hall
places.summary: San Francisco Landmark No. 277, designated in 2018, at 2117-2123 Market Street.
places.history: No source states an occupancy history of the building, so none is given here.

places.name: Alfred E. "Nobby" Clarke Mansion
places.summary: A mansion at 250 Douglass Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 80, designated in 1975. No visiting arrangements are published for it.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its designation under Article 10.

places.name: The McCormick House
places.summary: A house at 4040 17th Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 208, designated in 2000. Exterior only.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its designation under Article 10.

places.name: Benedict-Gieling House
places.summary: A house at 22 Beaver Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 284, designated in 2019. Exterior only.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its designation under Article 10.

places.name: Saint Francis Lutheran Church
places.summary: A working church at 152 Church Street that a visitor can enter. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 39, designated in 1971. No source states its opening hours or service times, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a congregational history, so none is given here.

places.name: Miller-Joost House
places.summary: A house on Upper Market at 3224 Market Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 79, designated in 1975. Exterior only.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its designation under Article 10.

places.name: St. Nicholas Cathedral
places.summary: A working cathedral church that a visitor can enter. San Francisco Landmark No. 335, designated in 2026, at 2005 15th Street.
places.history: The enacting ordinance is No. 73-26, carrying a Board of Supervisors memorandum dated 15 May 2026. No source states its service times, so none are given here.

places.name: GLBT Historical Society Museum
places.summary: A museum of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender history at 4127 18th Street, telephone (415) 777-5455. Its own site gives the hours as Tuesday to Sunday, 11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. and 1:30 p.m. to 5:00 p.m., closed Monday. Admission is free to all visitors on the first Wednesday of every month, sponsored by the Bob Ross Foundation.
places.history: The museum opened for previews on 10 December 2010 and had its grand opening on 13 January 2011. It is a project of the GLBT Historical Society, whose archive collections are held at a separate address outside this district.

places.name: Randall Museum
places.summary: A free children's and natural-science museum standing inside Corona Heights Park, owned and operated by San Francisco Recreation and Parks. Its own site gives Tuesday through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed Sunday and Monday, admission free, telephone (415) 554-9600. Cafe Josephine inside it opens Tuesday to Friday 9:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. and Saturday 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m.
places.history: The institution was established in 1937 as the Junior Museum, in a former city jail on what is now the City College campus. It opened at the Corona Heights site in 1951, in a building by the architect William Merchant, and was dedicated by Mayor Elmer Robinson on 23 September 1951 as the Josephine D. Randall Junior Museum.

places.name: Eureka Valley / Harvey Milk Memorial Branch Library
places.address: 1 Jose Sarria Court, San Francisco, CA 94114
places.summary: A San Francisco Public Library branch at 1 Jose Sarria Court, telephone 415-355-5616. Its hours are Sunday 1 to 5, Monday 10 to 6, Tuesday 10 to 8, Wednesday 10 to 8, Thursday 10 to 8, Friday 1 to 6 and Saturday 10 to 6.
places.history: A separate garden parcel on 16th Street carries the branch's name in the city's property records; it is a community garden and not the library building.

places.name: Corona Heights Park
places.summary: A 13.25-acre hill park with an unobstructed panoramic view from its summit. The Recreation and Parks Department gives the park entrance as Roosevelt and Museum Way and the park hours as 5 a.m. to midnight. A one-mile trail network winds to the summit, and the descent to the 15th Street tennis courts runs about 0.2 of a mile. The steps leading up to the peak are not supported by handrails.
places.history: The hill is Franciscan chert, exposed terra-cotta red at the summit; the base of the hill is about 300 feet above sea level and the peak about 520 feet. Bill Kraus Meadow, a triangular shaped patch of lawn at the park entrance at Museum Way and Roosevelt Way, and the Bill Kraus Pathway leading to the off-leash dog area were dedicated in his honour in 1986. The Randall Museum stands inside the park, and the park adjoins Buena Vista Park.

places.name: States Street Playground
places.summary: A 2.91-acre neighbourhood park and playground at 122 States Street. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the park.

places.name: Eureka Valley Recreation Center
places.summary: A 2.25-acre recreation ground at 100 Collingwood Street, carried in the city's property records as a neighbourhood park or playground. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the facility.

places.name: Peixotto Playground
places.summary: A 0.82-acre playground at 2475 15th Street. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the playground.

places.name: Roosevelt and Henry Stairs
places.summary: A 0.39-acre mini park at 299 Henry Street, carrying a public stairway between Roosevelt Way and Henry Street.
places.history: No source states a history of the stairway.

places.name: Saturn Street Steps
places.summary: A 0.19-acre mini park at 70 Ord Street, carrying a public stairway on Saturn Street.
places.history: No source states a history of the stairway.

places.name: Noe and Beaver Mini Park
places.summary: A 0.11-acre mini park at 1 Beaver Street, at the corner of Noe and Beaver Streets.
places.history: No source states a history of the park.

places.name: Pink Triangle Park and Memorial
places.summary: A memorial garden at Castro, Market and 17th Streets, holding 15 granite pylons, each of which represents 1,000 lives lost. A loose rock-filled triangle at its centre holds rose crystals, and visitors are encouraged to take one. It is run by volunteers through a 501(c)(3) organisation, and its own site titles it the Pink Triangle Memorial.
places.history: It was dedicated on 10 December 2001, United Nations Human Rights Day, by the Eureka Valley Promotion Association. Its own site states that 100,000 men were arrested between 1933 and 1945.

places.name: Rainbow Honor Walk
places.summary: Bronze plaques set into the sidewalks of Castro Street, with a self-guided tour published on the walk's own site. Its counters give 46 plaques installed and 28 planned, with fundraising continuing. The route runs from the Harvey Milk Civil Rights Academy at 19th and Collingwood along Castro Street to Market, and the walk branches in both directions at 18th and Castro.
places.history: The walk was founded by David Perry. A first round of twenty plaques was installed in 2014 and a second round of twenty-four was completed in 2019; twenty-four further honorees were named in 2022. The Castro Street History Walk shares the same pavement: twenty historical fact plaques, ten of them covering the period from before 1776 to the 1960s and ten covering events associated with the queer community in the Castro, contained within the 400 and 500 blocks of Castro Street between 19th and Market. The paving they sit in was laid by the Castro Street Streetscape Improvement Project, which San Francisco Public Works records as completed, on Castro Street between Market and 19th Streets, at a budget of ten million dollars in District 8, funded by the 2011 Road Repaving and Street Safety Bond and the Federal Transportation Administration.

places.name: Most Holy Redeemer Catholic Church
places.summary: A working Catholic parish at 100 Diamond Street, parish office (415) 863-6259. Its own site gives Mass Monday to Friday at 8:00 a.m., a Saturday vigil at 5:00 p.m., Sunday at 8:00 a.m., 10:00 a.m. and 6:30 p.m., holy days at 8:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m., and Thanksgiving Day at 10:00 a.m. Reconciliation is on Saturdays from 3:45 to 4:30 p.m.
places.history: The parish site names a Commemorative Wall and Fountain and an MHR AIDS Memorial among its features. The parish is the subject of a book on the inclusion of the gay community in a Catholic parish, Donal Godfrey's Gays and Grays, published by Lexington Books in 2008.

places.name: Castro Country Club
places.summary: A sober community coffeehouse and recovery space at 4058 18th Street, telephone 415-552-6102. Its own site gives the hours as Sunday to Thursday 7:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., and Friday and Saturday 7:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m.
places.history: No source states a history of the club, so none is given here.

places.name: Cliff's Variety
places.summary: A hardware and variety store at 471-479 Castro Street, telephone (415) 431-5365. Its own site gives the hours as Monday to Saturday 10:00 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. and Sunday 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., and names its counter services: keying and lock repair, knife sharpening, glass, acrylic and wood cutting, pipe threading and cable crimping.
places.history: Cliff's Variety moved into 479 Castro Street, the remodelled 1910 Castro Theatre building, in 1971.

places.history: Its neighbour at 220 Dolores Street carries its own number, San Francisco Landmark No. 68, designated in the same year.

links.note: The district east across Dolores Street, holding Mission San Francisco de Asis and Mission Dolores Park.
Corona Heights Park adjoins Buena Vista Park, which is on Haight Street, and the 2026 Article 10 designations run across both districts.
The next district along Market Street, holding the Carmel Fallon Building at 1800-1806 Market Street and the performing-arts halls on Van Ness Avenue.
